newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's Moi slams IMF aid decision as political.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's Moi slams IMF aid decision as political.

text.p: Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi on Sunday angrily condemned an International Monetary Fund (IMF) decision to cancel a big aid package as purely political and lacking economic sense.
In his first comment since the IMF ruling on Thursday, Moi said: "The stoppage of financial aid to Kenya by the IMF was purely political and has no economic rationality."

The Presidential Press Service (PPS) quoted Moi as saying he had undertaken painful economic reforms often at great cost both socially and politically. Moi has always contended that reforms severely hurt a majority of Kenya's 29 million population , 46 percent of whom live below the poverty line.

"Noting that the international community was not supportive of Africa's economy, President Moi recalled that he had on many occasions discussed social dimension issues with a former World Bank Vice-President Edward Jaycox," the PPS reported.
"The President observed that conditionalities imposed on Kenya disregarded these social dimensions and were therefore hurting Kenyans severely," the PPS added.

The IMF suspended a $205 million three-year loan to Kenya, citing concerns over corruption and reform of the energy sector in a decision that rocked Kenya's equity and foreign exchange markets and put the issue of corruption sharply in focus.

Moi, 73 and in power since 1978, faces elections this year which pit his ruling KANU party against an opposition that has found fragile cohesion in a campaign for constitutional reform. No election date has been set.

Nairobi newspapers said on Sunday that at the heart of the IMF decision was the refusal by Kenyan authorities to reinstate Commissioner of Customs and Excise Samuel Chebii, removed from his post while investigating massive fraud in sugar imports.
The Sunday Nation said Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi had told the IMF that Chebii would be reinstated and other IMF concerns would be addressed, but that he was later overruled by Moi.

The IMF also focused on a scandal involving Goldenberg International to show how authorities were wary about cracking down on corruption. Goldenberg was paid about $100 million by the government in 1992 under a compensation scheme for gold and diamond exports. Kenya produces little gold and no diamonds.

In an apparent reference to the Chebii case, PPS said: "He (Moi) said it was a pity that even Kenyan public servants entered this political arena without knowing the consequences. Moi reminded all public servants that at the end of the day they are answerable to the government."

Columnist Kwendo Opanga wrote in the Sunday Nation: "The reason why government is unwilling to punish corruption is that it is highly-placed government officials and powerful politically-connected individuals who are the culprits."

He added: "The reason corruption has run rampant in Kenya is that these people know they will be protected by government and will go scot-free. The IMF has been saying that the cases of corruption are simple and straightforward and should be dealt with expeditiously. Government does not want to expose itself."

The East African weekly, to be published on Monday, said $300-500 million held by foreign investors in "hot money" -- mainly government securities -- would be withdrawn at the first opportunity, fuelling pressure on the shilling.

It said investors would keenly await a decision on bilateral aid by Germany and Japan, among Kenya's largest creditors, as well as the World Bank which has approved but not disbursed a $125 million loan for Kenya's energy sector development.

The IMF ruling has forced the government to tighten belts amid fears of long-term damage to the economy. Minister Mudavadi said it had expected $215 million from the IMF and other donors in this financial year before the IMF decision on Thursday.
"The government will concurrently cut its expenditure for this year and take revenue measures sufficient to address the shortfall of $141 million in external funding," he said.
On Friday, Attorney-General Amos Wako published a tough anti-corruption bill to be debated and approved by parliament. Opposition leaders said they were suspicious of Wako's bills.

Foreign investors and tourists were already rattled by clashes between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators in June and July which culminated on July 7 with the deaths of at least nine people in Kenya's worst political unrest for seven years.
The shilling fell to around 62.50 versus the dollar at close on Friday from 59. Foreign exchange shops sold it at as low as 65 on Sunday, signalling that it would be under pressure on Monday.

Kenya's Association of Manufacturers said in a joint statement with the Chamber of Commerce and Industry and corporate executive Chris Kirubi that the IMF decision was very unfortunate and urged the government to return to talks.
